history.heading: Settlement
paragraphs: Réunion, a volcanic island in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar, was uninhabited when Arab and later Portuguese sailors found it. France claimed it in the 17th century, naming it Île Bourbon, and settlers established coffee and later sugar plantations worked by enslaved people from Madagascar, East Africa and India.

The island was renamed Réunion during the French Revolution. Slavery was abolished on 20 December 1848, a date still celebrated as a holiday, after which indentured workers came from India, China and elsewhere.

history.heading: French department
paragraphs: Réunion became an overseas department of France in 1946. From 1963 to 1982, about 2,000 children were forcibly moved to rural mainland France, a scandal known as the "Children of Creuse", for which France apologised in 2014.

culture.heading: Creole melting pot
paragraphs: French is official, and Réunion Creole is spoken by most people. The population blends African, Malagasy, Indian (Tamil and Gujarati Muslim), Chinese and European ancestry. Catholicism, Hinduism and Islam coexist.

Maloya, music and dance born among enslaved people, is recognised by UNESCO. Rougail and cari (curry) are signature dishes. The island's volcanic peaks, cirques and Piton de la Fournaise, one of the world's most active volcanoes, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

politics.heading: Part of France
paragraphs: Réunion is an overseas department and region of France and an outermost region of the European Union. It has a regional council and a departmental council and elects members to the French parliament.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: The economy depends on public services, French transfers, tourism and agriculture, especially sugar cane and rum, as well as vanilla and geranium oil. Unemployment, particularly among young people, is far higher than in mainland France, and the cost of living is high. The currency is the euro.
